core1a.phenomenon: Two instruments can play the same note yet sound different, and a modified instrument may change pitch or loudness independently.
core1a.scientific_narrative:
A musical instrument is a system that excites mechanical vibration and couples it to the surrounding medium. A string instrument can be plucked or bowed; a membrane can be struck; a reed or air jet can excite an air column. The vibrating object and the air that carries sound to the listener are not the same thing. A sounding board may couple a vibrating string more effectively to air, changing radiated sound without requiring the fundamental frequency to change.

Pitch is associated mainly with repetition frequency or fundamental frequency for a simple periodic tone. Timbre describes differences in sound quality arising in part from the relative strengths of frequency components, their evolution in time and the attack/decay envelope. Two instruments may produce the same fundamental frequency but different overtones and envelopes; a listener may distinguish them even at similar pitch and loudness. A microphone spectrum is an instrument-dependent measurement: compare calibrated or consistently normalized data before attributing amplitude differences to the source. Loudness is a perceptual quantity, not directly a spectral peak height.

Changing an instrument can affect several variables at once. Shortening the vibrating length of an ideal string at fixed tension and mass per length raises its fundamental frequency. Tightening a string at fixed length and mass per length also raises its fundamental, whereas increasing mass per length lowers it. In an ideal fixed-end string, f=(1/(2L))√(F/μ). This formula is an explicitly supplied enrichment model; the qualitative instrument lesson does not require detailed standing-wave theory. For air columns, effective vibrating length and open/closed boundary conditions affect resonant frequencies; an open hole can change effective length, but real end corrections and geometry matter. Do not use the string formula for an air column.

When a string is plucked harder, its initial amplitude and radiated sound may increase, but in the small-amplitude linear approximation its normal frequencies do not change solely because of amplitude. A real string can change tension or effective stiffness at large amplitude, so the ideal claim has a limit. Compare equal source conditions and measure both the temporal period and spectrum; if an altered body changes coupling, a source-motion measurement can distinguish frequency change from radiation change. A spectrum showing peaks at integer multiples of a fundamental suggests a harmonic structure, but one measured peak alone need not identify the fundamental or the instrument.

A fair instrument comparison records source length, tension or boundary conditions, excitation, receiver position and sensor calibration. A controlled intervention and independent observation can distinguish a shifted resonant frequency from stronger excitation or changed acoustic coupling. The exact Core2 bank has no matching instrument question; all tasks are authored learning transfer.

progressive_examples.problem: Two tones repeat every4 ms; their waveforms have different shapes. Compare fundamental frequency and possible timbre.
progressive_examples.independent_check: Different shapes can contain different spectral components.

progressive_examples.problem: A string's vibrating length halves at fixed tension and linear density. What happens to ideal fundamental?
At fixed length and μ, tension quadruples; pluck amplitude also changes. Ideal f was150 Hz. Predict new fundamental.
progressive_examples.reasoning: 300 Hz, independent of amplitude in linear model.
progressive_examples.independent_check: √4=2; check whether real tension changes during vibration.

misconception.wrong_model: Higher amplitude means higher pitch, and equal pitch means identical instrument.
misconception.diagnostic: Can two waveforms have equal repetition period but different spectral composition?
misconception.repair: Measure period and spectral components separately, and control the vibrating geometry and coupling.

exit_check.task: An ideal string's length doubles while tension quadruples at fixed μ. Compare fundamental.
exit_check.reasoning: Length factor1/2 and tension factor√4=2 cancel.

core1b.fresh_task: A string attached to a larger sounding body produces stronger microphone output, while its measured vibration period and length remain unchanged. Explain why pitch need not change and why stronger output does not prove the string vibrates with larger displacement.
core1b.protected_work: Explain an instrument modification by tracing excitation, mode frequency and radiation coupling as separate causal links.

stages.predict: Predict whether the stronger microphone signal necessarily means higher pitch.
stages.attempt: A string attached to a larger sounding body produces stronger microphone output, while its measured vibration period and length remain unchanged. Explain why pitch need not change and why stronger output does not prove the string vibrates with larger displacement.
stages.reconstruct: Coupling/radiation changes can strengthen output; equal period supports same fundamental. Measure actual displacement independently, control microphone and position.
stages.diagnose: Check whether you used receiver loudness to infer source frequency or ignored a changed acoustic boundary.
stages.repair: Trace vibration, mode frequency and coupling separately, then identify a direct observation for each inference.
stages.boundary_test: If the body changes string tension, can the same pitch prediction be assumed?

core1b.fresh_task: A wind instrument plays a higher note when a hole is opened. Its microphone amplitude decreases. Explain how effective vibrating air-column length and radiation/detection can lead to different pitch and amplitude trends.
core1b.protected_work: Explain an instrument modification by tracing excitation, mode frequency and radiation coupling as separate causal links.

stages.predict: Predict whether pitch and microphone amplitude must change in the same direction.
stages.attempt: A wind instrument plays a higher note when a hole is opened. Its microphone amplitude decreases. Explain how effective vibrating air-column length and radiation/detection can lead to different pitch and amplitude trends.
stages.reconstruct: Opening hole can shorten effective acoustic length and raise resonance; output amplitude depends on excitation and coupling, not frequency alone. Boundary details need control.
stages.diagnose: Check whether you used receiver loudness to infer source frequency or ignored a changed acoustic boundary.
stages.repair: Trace vibration, mode frequency and coupling separately, then identify a direct observation for each inference.
stages.boundary_test: If opening the hole changes the boundary type as well as length, is a simple inverse-length comparison sufficient?

core1b.fresh_task: A string gives200 Hz. Its vibrating length becomes half and tension becomes one quarter; μ unchanged. A sensor records200 Hz. Compare a length-only model and the supplied ideal combined model; predict f if tension is restored while length stays half.
core1b.protected_work: Choose and test a specified ideal instrument frequency model against independent length/tension observations, distinguishing it from amplitude-only or length-only explanations.

stages.predict: Predict whether shortening alone determines the new pitch when tension also changes.
stages.attempt: A string gives200 Hz. Its vibrating length becomes half and tension becomes one quarter; μ unchanged. A sensor records200 Hz. Compare a length-only model and the supplied ideal combined model; predict f if tension is restored while length stays half.
stages.reconstruct: Length-only predicts400; combined predicts200, fits. Restored tension at half length gives400 Hz under model.
stages.diagnose: Find whether your frequency prediction ignored a changed parameter or used an untested idealization as proof.
stages.repair: Compute the separate length and tension factors, compare model predictions with measured frequency, and reserve a new condition to test.
stages.boundary_test: If μ also doubles during the final modification, what frequency follows?

core1b.fresh_task: Two recordings have the same fundamental and peak amplitude, but one has strong second and third harmonics while the other does not. A report says they must sound identical. Assess and propose a matched comparison.
core1b.protected_work: Determine whether measured pitch or a limited spectrum uniquely establishes instrument identity or sound quality, using counterexamples and controlled evidence.

stages.predict: Predict whether matching fundamental and peak amplitude establish identical sound quality.
stages.attempt: Two recordings have the same fundamental and peak amplitude, but one has strong second and third harmonics while the other does not. A report says they must sound identical. Assess and propose a matched comparison.
stages.reconstruct: Equal fundamental suggests same pitch, not identical timbre; spectral strengths and envelope differ. Match level, microphone and playback conditions; compare calibrated spectra and envelopes.
stages.diagnose: Identify whether you treated a detected component as the guaranteed fundamental or a fundamental as a unique source signature.
stages.repair: Construct compatible alternate sources, then specify a broader calibrated measurement and the exact conclusion it can support.
stages.boundary_test: If full steady-state magnitude spectra match, does that alone establish identical time-domain signals?

stages.predict: Would you infer identical fundamental and source from the single detected peak?
stages.attempt: Two instruments produce spectra with only one detected peak at400 Hz under a narrow-band sensor. A technician concludes they must share the same fundamental and instrument type. Construct two compatible source explanations and specify an improved measurement.
stages.reconstruct: 400 Hz could be fundamental of one and second harmonic of a 200 Hz source whose fundamental is filtered/weak. Different instruments can share components. Use calibrated broadband time/spectrum and source observations.
